title: Are pets called 'pets' because we pet them?

entries.note: From Scottish Gaelic or Irish for a domesticated animal; it first meant a hand-reared lamb, and the verb to pet (stroke) came later, in the 1600s.
British swimming pool signs saying no heavy petting meant no snogging, because in Britain you stroke a pet rather than [[see:pet]] it.
Given as one of the few English words from Scottish Gaelic, like [[see:pet]].
An animal abandoned by its mother and reared by hand; Johnson's dictionary defines [[see:pet]] as a cade lamb, and the two were used almost interchangeably.
An ironic use of [[see:pet]] in its sense of favourite: your favourite worst thing.
Affectionate names for someone you like, already established by the time the verb sense of [[see:pet]] appeared.
Illustrates the favouritism in the old sense of [[see:pet]] as a spoilt child.
Of unknown origin, one of the Old English words ending in a doubled G; it likely began as a cutesy diminutive that replaced [[see:hound]].
Another animal word with the unexplained final G sound, like [[see:dog]]; it replaced the older [[see:frosc]].
Another animal word with the unexplained final G sound, like [[see:dog]].
Another G-final animal word, like [[see:dog]], apparently a diminutive that replaced [[see:swine]].
Another animal word with the unexplained final G sound, like [[see:dog]].
Borrowed from English [[see:dog]], it usually means a mastiff, since mastiffs were the dogs most associated with Britain.
The older general word for a dog, which swapped places with [[see:dog]] and became the more specific, breed-centred term.
The older word for a frog, recognisable to German speakers, replaced by the diminutive [[see:frog]].
The older word for the animal now generally called a [[see:pig]].
Means dwarf dog in Welsh.
Means badger hound, from German [[from:Dachs]], because the breed was used to chase badgers out of their holes.
Old French mastin meant great [[see:cur]], but it comes from a Latin word meaning tame or gentle.
A 13th-century word for a dog, usually a badly behaved or ill-bred one, supposedly from a root meaning growl.
From Middle English [[from:fisting cur]], farting dog; it described vivacious little dogs, reportedly after ladies blamed their farts on their lapdogs.
Usually translated little brushwood dog, perhaps for the landscape it hunted in or for its golden coat.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning plunge earth, supposedly because the dogs leapt off camels' backs while hunting.
Named after puddles, from German [[from:Pudelhund]], since they were bred as water dogs with quick-drying curly coats.
Jess's puppy's breed, also called mini Aussie, now recognised as a breed in its own right and accurately named, unlike the [[see:Australian Shepherd]].
A false name: neither Australian Shepherds nor mini Aussies are actually Australian.
From French [[from:poupée]], doll, perhaps because little dogs were playthings; related to [[same-root:puppet]] and [[same-root:poppet]], and it replaced [[see:whelp]].
Related to [[same-root:puppy]].
A British term of endearment related to [[same-root:puppy]].
The earlier word for baby dogs, supplanted by [[see:puppy]].
From the Book of St Albans, the first written use of litter as a collective noun for puppies, tongue-in-cheek like the book's other collective nouns.
Another tongue-in-cheek collective noun, like [[see:litter of whelps]].
Another tongue-in-cheek collective noun, like [[see:litter of whelps]].
Another collective noun in the same book as [[see:litter of whelps]], and one Jess loves.
Probably a variation on French [[from:chaton]], little cat.
Similar words across many European language families probably arose independently from imitation rather than a common root; Late Latin [[see:cattus]] may be North African.
The French word for cat, basically [[same-root:cat]] with an H in it.
Many languages have similar words for it because they imitate the same sound, which may explain the similar words for [[see:cat]].
A sound used to call a cat, another imitative word like [[see:meow]].
A Late Latin word for cat that may come from North Africa, where Nubian and Berber languages have similar words; it supports the imitative theory for [[see:cat]].
The classical Latin word for cat, which gave [[gave:feline]], older than [[see:cattus]].
Comes from Latin [[from:felis]].
Rob decides it is fine to say theory where hypothesis is the scientifically correct word, since everyone does.
From [[from:attabi]], a striped silk made in the Attabiya district of Baghdad; the imported wavy-striped fabric gave its name to striped cats.
The general German word for a cat, while a male cat is a [[see:Kater]].
The German word for a male cat, which also means hangover, for reasons the hosts don't know.

entries.term: the hair of the dog that bit you
entries.note: First recorded in the 16th century for drinking to cure a hangover; the theoretical rabies cure seems to have been figurative from the start.
Its origin was explained, more than once, in the hosts' earlier episodes on dog and cat idioms.
First meant [[see:turtle dove]], imitating its cooing; it came to mean the reptile in the 1600s when French [[see:tortue]] was misheard as turtle.
From Middle English tortuse, with spelling influenced by [[see:porpoise]], and from Latin for twisted, perhaps for their feet, or possibly from [[from?:Tartarus]].
The order containing all turtles, tortoises and terrapins, from Latin [[from:testa]], shell.
Belongs to the turtle order [[see:Testudines]] along with turtles and tortoises.
What Old English [[see:turtle]] referred to, the word imitating its cooing; discussed in an earlier episode.
The French word for both turtle and tortoise, misheard in English as [[see:turtle]].
What aquatic turtles were called before [[see:turtle]] took on that meaning.
Its ending influenced the spelling of [[see:tortoise]], which Jess uses as a reverse mnemonic.
Related to [[same-root:tortoise]] through the sense of twisted.
Related to [[same-root:tortoise]] through the sense of twisted.
Probably related to [[same-root?:bovine]]; Pliny's mythical boa sucked cows' milk, and [[see:Linnaeus]] later applied the Latin name to the South American constrictor.
Probably related to [[same-root?:boa constrictor]], since the mythical boa drank cows' milk or killed cows.
Named after its loud call, probably via a Malay or Japanese imitation of the sound.
Probably Persian and meaning inside flame, because salamanders crawled out of rotting logs thrown on fires; in heraldry it looks more like a dragon.
A type of salamander, now popular online, whose name is a Nahuatl (Aztec) word.
Means ground lion, though its eyes and colour-changing hardly suggest a lion.
The French word for a bat, which Rob thinks should be flying mouse, like [[equivalent:flittermouse]].
An old word for a bat, preferred by the hosts to [[equivalent:chauve-souris]].
Covered before; it means the same as flutter, like [[see:flittermouse]].
From German, via Old High German [[from:hamustro]] and Russian [[from:khomyak]], from an Iranian source like Avestan [[from:hamaestar]], one who tramples down, meaning a crop pest.
Shopping like a [[see:hamster]], meaning hoarding more than you need; it came up a lot during the pandemic.
The collective noun for hamsters, in the army sense rather than hoarding, which fits the trampling sense of [[see:hamster]].
The English name for the [[see:hamster]] before the word hamster was adopted.
Neither a pig nor from Guinea; perhaps named after the [[from?:guinea hog]], or after [[see:Guinea]] as a generic far-off land.
A pig thought to come from Guinea that didn't, and a possible source of [[gave?:guinea pig]].
Besides the African place, it once meant any far-off land, and slave ships were colloquially called Guinea, so exotic imports were said to come from Guinea.
Actually does come from Guinea; guinea fowl were first called [[see:turkey]]s.
First the name of the [[see:guinea fowl]], because Turkish traders sold them into Europe, before it named the North American bird.
Probably from an Indigenous Peruvian language, Aymara or Quechua, reshaped to look like a Spanish diminutive.
From Latin [[from:gerbillus]], a diminutive of [[from:jerboa]]; ultimately a Berber and Arabic word puzzlingly meaning flesh of the loins.
A springy animal a bit like a large gerbil, whose diminutive gave [[gave:gerbil]].
Named after mice running under the skin, offered as a parallel to the flesh-of-the-loins meaning behind [[see:gerbil]].
Ultimately from a word meaning robber, taken from French [[from:furet]], which Rob links to [[see?:fuir]], to flee.
Meant sending your hunting [[see:ferret]] after an animal, since ferrets were domesticated to chase rabbits from warrens.
The collective noun for ferrets, a favourite of the hosts.
An Australian term, which leads to the origin of [[see:budgerigar]].
From an unidentified Australian Aboriginal language, combining words for good and cockatoo, so basically good parrot; Americans call them [[see:parakeet]]s.
The American name for budgies, related to [[same-root:parrot]] and possibly from Italian [[from?:perrucchetto]], little wig, after their feather tufts.
From Middle French [[from:Perrot]], a diminutive of [[from:Pierre]] used as an epithet for a talker, paralleling [[see:robin]].
Linked to the Italian word for little wig that may lie behind [[see:parakeet]].
Formed from [[from:lory]] plus the -keet of [[see:parakeet]], an example of a [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
A Malay word for the bird, which was given the -keet ending to make [[gave:lorikeet]].
A morpheme that only belongs to its own word and can't be moved elsewhere, like the cran of [[see:cranberry]] or the rasp of [[see:raspberry]].
Cran comes from crane, because the plant's flowers look like little crane heads; the classic [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
Its rasp is thought to be unrelated to a rasping throat, making it a [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
Another example of a [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
A unit of a word, a bit like but not quite a syllable.
Originally a diminutive of [[from:Robert]], paralleling [[see:parrot]] from a pet form of Pierre.
Pie was the original name; mag, short for Margaret and an epithet for a chatty woman, refers to the bird's chattiness.
Named after the [[from:Canary Islands]], which are named after dogs, so it is indirectly a dog bird.
From Latin for island of dogs; the islands gave their name to the [[gave:canary]].
A familiar human nickname, a variant of Molly and Mary, linking talkative birds and women; popularised partly by [[see:Andrew Jackson]]'s swearing parrot Poll.
Had a grey parrot called Poll that reportedly swore loudly at his funeral, helping popularise [[see:Polly]].
A classic dog name meaning faithful or trustworthy, related to [[same-root:fidelity]].
Compared with [[same-root:Fido]].
A dog that roves, popularised by the 1905 British film [[see:Rescued by Rover]].
A 1905 British film where a dog rescues a kidnapped baby, sparking a fashion for naming dogs [[see:Rover]].
Jess's dog, whose name means much the same as [[see:Rover]] and nods to [[see:Aragorn]] because of his long legs and white chest spot.
The Lord of the Rings character nicknamed Longshanks, the inspiration for [[see:Ranger]].
A common cat name meaning happy or lucky, popular thanks to [[see:Felix the Cat]] and its resemblance to Latin [[see:felis]].
The cartoon cat mostly responsible for the popularity of [[see:Felix]] as a cat name.
One of Taylor Swift's three cats, as of a 2020 article.
One of Taylor Swift's three cats, as of a 2020 article.
One of Taylor Swift's three cats, as of a 2020 article.
Miley Cyrus's pet pig.
Justin Bieber's capuchin monkey, named after the rapper Mally Mall who gave it; confiscated in Munich over paperwork, it now lives in a Danish reserve.
George Clooney's 300-pound pot-bellied pig.
One of Reese Witherspoon's two donkeys, the other being [[see:Donkey]].
One of Reese Witherspoon's two donkeys, the other being [[see:Honky]].
Vanilla Ice's pet [[see:wallaroo]].
An animal between a wallaby and a kangaroo in size, like Vanilla Ice's pet [[see:Bucky]].
Audrey Hepburn's pet fawn, which apparently slept in her bed.
Salvador Dalí's pet ocelot; his famous anteater was borrowed from the zoo for the day, in homage to André Breton.
Samuel Johnson's cat, which has a statue thanks to one of Johnson's biographers rather than Johnson himself.
Charles Dickens's thieving raven, said to have inspired Poe's [[see:The Raven]]; now preserved by taxidermy in Philadelphia.
Poe's poem, said to have been inspired by Dickens's raven [[see:Grip]].
Emily Brontë's cat, a fitting name for a cat, jokingly fiddling with yarn as Rome burned.
